name: Norse religion
areas: the lands around Uppsala, the last stronghold of the old gods
the Varangians of the river routes
pagan worship allowed in private for a time
routes: The Great Army settles the Danelaw (865)
marks: The royal mounds of Gamla Uppsala (6th century) mark a great centre of the old gods in Sweden.
A royal seat in Denmark, where Thietmar of Merseburg (around 1015) placed great sacrifices every nine years.
The Viking raid on the monastery here (793) opens the Viking Age.
King Harald Bluetooth raised the Jelling stone, recording that he made the Danes Christian (around 965).
The Althing adopted Christianity here around 1000, allowing pagan worship in private for a time.
Olaf Haraldsson fell here in 1030; venerated as a saint, he became the symbol of Christian Norway.
Adam of Bremen describes the temple at Uppsala with images of Thor, Odin and Freyr (around 1075), one of the last centres of the old religion.
notes: The peoples of Scandinavia worship Odin, Thor, Freyr and other gods at open-air sites and in halls; great mounds are raised at Uppsala.
Picture stones on Gotland and small gold foil figures show gods, heroes and rites.
The Viking raid on Lindisfarne (793) opens the Viking Age.
Vikings settle the Danelaw in England (865), Iceland (874) and the river routes of Rus'; missionaries such as Ansgar preach in Denmark and Sweden.
Harald Bluetooth makes the Danes Christian (around 965); Norse settlers in England, Normandy and Rus' take up Christianity; Erik the Red settles Greenland (985).
Iceland adopts Christianity (around 1000) and Norway under Olaf (d. 1030); in Sweden the temple at Uppsala still stands around 1075, the last great centre of the old gods.
Scandinavia is Christian by the 12th century; the old myths survive in the poems and sagas written down in Iceland in the 13th century.
src: John Lindow, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (2001)
Anders Andrén, Kristina Jennbert and Catharina Raudvere (eds), Old Norse Religion in Long-Term Perspectives (2006)
Neil Price, Children of Ash and Elm: A History of the Vikings (2020)
